title: Mudita
hook: sympathetic joy: gladness at someone else's good fortune

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion for the one who harms, and your line: they are heading for pain. Could you wish someone a different road? Day two hundred thirty-eight, the end of the week, and the third room.
screen: `COMPASSION FOR THE ONE WHO HARMS — THEY ARE HEADING FOR PAIN.`

segments.voice: A friend texts: I got the job. Or: we're engaged. Or: the scan was clear. And for a split second, before you type the exclamation points, notice what happens inside. Sometimes it's pure gladness. Sometimes there's a small, uninvited flicker: why not me? Its darker cousin, pleasure at someone else's trouble, is familiar enough that English borrowed a German word for it. For the good opposite, joy at someone else's good fortune, English has no everyday word at all. Pali does. Today: mudita.
screen: `I GOT THE JOB.` → `A SMALL FLICKER: WHY NOT ME?` → `ENGLISH HAS NO WORD.`

segments.voice: Mudita comes from a root meaning to be glad, to rejoice. It's usually translated sympathetic joy, or appreciative joy: gladness at another's happiness and success. It's the third of the four rooms. The Visuddhimagga's map says mudita's mark is gladness, and its job is to be free of envy. It shows up as the end of discontent, the sour feeling that someone else's good news somehow takes something away from you. Its ground is seeing other people's success. Here's what makes mudita unusual. Kindness wishes that people be happy. Compassion wishes that they be free from pain. Mudita meets people who already are happy, and simply agrees. It's joy you didn't have to earn, available every time anyone, anywhere, has a good day. Some teachers call it the most overlooked of the four rooms, because we assume we'd feel it naturally, and then discover the little flicker of why not me. The manual has practical advice. Start with someone you're already close to, a dear friend whose good news makes you easily glad. Then widen the circle: a neutral person, then someone difficult. And it suggests practicing when you see someone happy, or hear good news about them, so the gladness has something real to rest on. This week you walked through two and a half rooms. The four divine abodes. Metta, and its near enemy, clinging. Its far enemy, ill will. Karuna, the trembling heart. Pity, which looks down, and compassion, which sits beside. Compassion even for the one who harms. Now mudita: their joy is joy, and it can be yours too.
screen: `MUDITA — GLADNESS, REJOICING.` · `THE MARK: GLADNESS; THE JOB: NO ENVY.` · `JOY YOU DIDN'T HAVE TO EARN.` · `START WITH A DEAR FRIEND.` · then, large: `THEIR JOY IS JOY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a dear friend who's had some good news lately, or who's simply happy right now. Picture their face when things are going well. Let yourself be glad with them. If words help, offer one: may your happiness continue. Notice how it feels in your own body to be glad for someone. Then, if you like, widen it: someone you barely know, enjoying a good day. Their joy, yours too. The bell holds the time.
Mudita. Sympathetic joy: gladness at someone else's good fortune, joy you didn't have to earn.
Your line: their joy is joy. Today, congratulate someone sincerely, and let yourself enjoy their good news for a whole breath. Day two hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Buddhists practice mudita by rejoicing in others' happiness and good deeds; in many Theravada communities people say 'sadhu, sadhu, sadhu' to rejoice in someone else's merit, and teachers offer mudita as a meditation starting with a dear friend.

original.note: Pali and Sanskrit muditā: sympathetic joy, the third divine abode.

trapdoor: what you thought: mudita means being happy.
what it means: gladness at someone else's good fortune: joy you didn't have to earn.
what a scholar hears: Visuddhimagga IX gives mudita's characteristic as gladness, its function as being unenvious, its manifestation as the elimination of aversion (arati).

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga IX (mudita: characteristic, function, manifestation, order of persons)

notes: Visuddhimagga IX.95 paraphrased (characteristic gladness; function being unenvious; manifestation elimination of aversion/boredom, arati; proximate cause seeing beings' success). Confirm.
Order of persons for mudita (dear friend first): Vsm IX.84–86 recommend a 'very dear companion' as the first object; confirm.
The hook alludes to Schadenfreude without naming it.
'Sadhu, sadhu, sadhu' as rejoicing in merit (anumodana) is common Theravada usage.
Week-end look-back (days 232–237) is in the teach.
Audit 2026-09-30: hook fixed; it said 'other languages have borrowed a word' for Schadenfreude, when it is English that borrowed the German word.
